passages.happening: Zechariah lifts up his eyes and sees a flying scroll, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide (verses 1-2). The angel tells him it is the curse that goes out over the whole land: by one side of it every thief will be removed, and by the other every one who swears falsely (verse 3). God will send it out, and it will enter the house of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by his name, and stay there until it destroys the house, timber and stones (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This is the sixth vision. Twenty cubits by ten is about thirty feet by fifteen, an enormous scroll, the size of the porch of Solomon's temple. Unrolled and flying, it can be read by everyone.

The two crimes named, theft and false swearing in God's name, stand for the two halves of the commandments: wrongs against a neighbor and wrongs against God. The covenant's curse, written in the law, goes out to find the guilty. As the temple is rebuilt, God is cleansing the land of wrongdoing as well as rebuilding stones.
passages.later: The commandments forbid both: ‘You shall not steal’ (Exodus 20:15) and taking the LORD's name in vain (Exodus 20:7). The porch of Solomon's temple was twenty cubits by ten (1 Kings 6:3).
passages.asks: The scroll of the curse flew into the houses of thieves and false swearers. Ask whether there is anything in your house God's word would find there. And ask how your treatment of others and your honesty before God belong together.

passages.t: Wickedness carried away in a basket
passages.happening:
The angel tells Zechariah to look, and he sees a measuring basket going out, which the angel says is the iniquity of the people throughout the land (verses 5-6). A lead cover is lifted, and a woman is sitting inside. ‘This is Wickedness,’ the angel says, and pushes her down into the basket and shoves the lead cover back over its mouth (verses 7-8).

Then two women come out with wind in their wings, wings like a stork's, and lift the basket between earth and sky (verse 9). Zechariah asks where they are taking it. To the land of Shinar, the angel says, to build a house for it; when it is ready, the basket will be set there on its base (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
This is the seventh vision. The measuring basket, an ephah, was a large container for grain. The lead cover shows how firmly wickedness is shut in. Shinar is the old name for Babylonia, where the tower of Babel was built. Wickedness is sent back where it belongs, far from the land God is cleansing, and given a house there, perhaps a temple with a pedestal for an idol.

The stork was a large, strong bird that migrates great distances, fit for carrying a heavy load far away.
passages.later: Shinar is where people built the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). Jeremiah condemned the worship of the Queen of Heaven (Jeremiah 44:17-19).
passages.hard:
Why is wickedness pictured as a woman, and does the passage demean women?

The simplest answer is grammatical. The Hebrew word for wickedness, rishah, is feminine, as many abstract nouns in Hebrew are, and prophetic visions often picture such nouns as women; Proverbs does the same with Wisdom and Folly. In the same vision, the agents God uses to carry wickedness away are also women, with wings, so the passage does not set women as such against God. Some scholars suggest a further background: the pedestal in Shinar may point to idol worship, and the woman may recall a goddess figure such as the Queen of Heaven condemned by Jeremiah, so that the vision pictures idolatry sent back to Babylon.

The vision is about wickedness removed from the land. It gives no one a reason to speak of women with contempt.
passages.asks: God shut wickedness in a basket and carried it far away. Ask what wrong you need God to remove from your life, not just to cover. And ask what it would mean to let go of something you have kept close.
